newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Left has a bad weekend in Eastern Europe.
newsitem.headline: Left has a bad weekend in Eastern Europe.

text.p: Eastern Europe's Left had a bad weekend, with Romanians dumping President Ion Iliescu and Czechs -- at least those who bothered to vote -- backing Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus's market reform.

While the pendulum sung further to the right in the former Soviet satellites, Belarus proved the ex-Soviet Union itself is often another story as riot police beat protesters trying to foil President Alexander Lukashenko's bid for greater power.
In recent years, the Left seemed almost unstoppable in eastern Europe with former communists regaining power in countries such as Poland, Hungary, Bulgaria and Lithuania.

Iliescu, the only ex-communist in the former East Bloc to have held uninterrupted power since 1989, seemed secure in Romania while the region's last conservative premier, Klaus, flirted with defeat when he lost his majority in June.
But a few weeks is a long time in post-communist politics.

In some countries, at least, the same voters who returned the Left to power in 1992-4 seem to be tiring of the failure of reformed communism to solve economic problems and deliver a gentler kind of reform.
In the past month Lithuanians and Romanians have returned centre-right governments to power and Bulgarians have voted resoundingly against an ex-communist presidential candidate.
Last weekend, Romanians completed their rout of the Left by dispatching Iliescu, a senior official under Stalinist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu who was deposed and executed in 1989.
Professor Emil Constantinescu beat Iliescu surprisingly easily on Sunday, promising supporters: "Romania will become again the dignified and prosperous country we all wanted."

But he also warned Romanians that the path would not be easy. "We will have an austerity programme. We have an extremely difficult legacy. The government must apply long-term reform but must achieve results quickly," he said.

It was this kind shock therapy which economists say delivered rapid growth in Poland, but allowed reformed communists to end rule by governments based on the anti-communist Solidarity movement in 1993.

In the Czech Republic, the centre-left also did badly in the first round of Senate elections on Friday and Saturday. Klaus's Civic Democratic Party (ODS) took 36.5 percent of the vote while the Social Democrats limped in with 20.3 percent.

Superficially at least, the result was a remarkable turnaround from lower house elections in June when the Social Democrats came within three percentage points of the ODS and stripped Klaus's centre-right coalition of its majority.
However, turnout was only 34 percent and analysts said the result indicated the superior ability of the ODS to get its supporters to vote for a new chamber which few Czechs seem to understand.
Klaus warned his supporters of the danger of an alliance of the Social Democrats, led by his archrival Milos Zeman, and the little-reformed Communists.
"We have noticed that (Zeman) tells his voters only one thing: don't vote ODS. We interpret that to mean in a number of cases he's saying: vote for the Communists," Klaus said.
In the former Soviet republic of Belarus, Lukashenko continued to resist the wind of change.
In Minsk, riot police beat protesters marching towards parliament, the focus of opposition to Lukashenko who is trying to gain more powers in a referendum next week.
Lukashenko sent voters a colour postcard of himself calling for their support.

"Mafia clans and the owners of ill-gotten capital have united against the president you elected," he wrote. "I turn to you, the honest people, to help save the country for the sake of our common future."
